chapter_title: Introduction to Web3.js and Provider Setup

screens.title: Introduction to Web3.js and Provider Setup
screens.subtitle: How your JavaScript dApp speaks to the Ethereum network

narration.text: Today we begin by making one core idea feel concrete: Web3. js is the translator that lets JavaScript-based dApps speak to an Ethereum node. You will learn what the library does, how a provider connects your code to a node, and why choosing the right provider matters for development, testing, and production. We’ll use a local development node for quick iteration, and a hosted provider for public networks, and we’ll also cover how browser wallets supply an in-browser provider. A clear mental model helps when debugging: imagine your dApp sending structured requests and receiving signed, verifiable responses from a node; Web3. js hides the low-level RPC plumbing so you can read state and send transactions with simple method calls. In practice, that means checking whether a node is listening, requesting accounts from a wallet, and using await to resolve asynchronous calls. By the end of this chapter you will be able to create a Web3 instance, confirm connectivity, fetch a network ID and block number, and diagnose the usual connection problems. Think of these skills as the networking foundation for any Ethereum dApp — without a reliable provider, higher-level features like token transfers or contract calls cannot function. Ready to see how that bridge is built and tested?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Web3.js is the library that abstracts RPC calls and provides an API for reading blockchain state and sending transactions; the provider is the actual network endpoint that enables this communication.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Introduction
Introduction to Web3.js
A practical orientation to connecting dApps to Ethereum nodes and why the provider matters.

Web3.js translates your JavaScript code into remote procedure calls that an Ethereum node understands. It helps you read blockchain state, request accounts, and submit transactions without composing raw RPC payloads.

Choosing between a local node, a hosted API, or an in-browser wallet provider changes where trust and security live. We’ll practice with Ganache and discuss hosted services and MetaMask.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you will demonstrate after this chapter

narration.text: In this chapter you will develop four practical competencies that let you connect and verify a dApp’s access to Ethereum. First, you will explain the role of Web3. js: why it exists, what RPC abstraction it provides, and how it removes low-level encoding from everyday development. Second, you will differentiate provider types: a local node for isolated testing, hosted providers for reliable public access, and in-browser wallet providers that connect with user accounts. Third, you will configure a Web3. js instance to connect to a chosen provider and use simple checks like the listening call to confirm connectivity. Fourth, you will identify and troubleshoot common issues: unreachable URLs, missing await on asynchronous calls, and absent injected providers in browsers. Each objective includes a clear mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you can self-assess. For instance, when you set up Web3 with Ganache and successfully fetch the network ID and block number, you have achieved the configuration milestone. These objectives are cumulative: understanding the role of the library helps you choose the right provider, and correct async handling and error checks make your connection robust. Keep these goals in mind as we build a small verification script and practice common fixes.

screens.title: What is Web3.js?
screens.subtitle: The JavaScript bridge for dApps and Ethereum nodes

narration.text: Start with a clear definition: Web3. js is a JavaScript library that exposes methods for reading blockchain state and submitting transactions to an Ethereum node. It wraps the low-level RPC protocol into familiar method calls so your front-end or Node. js code does not need to compose raw JSON-RPC requests. Practically, that means you can ask for an account balance, call a contract function, or send a signed transaction using straightforward methods rather than handcrafting and encoding payloads. A concrete example is fetching the latest block number: using the library’s method returns the block number as a resolved value when awaited. A common misconception is thinking Web3. js runs the blockchain or stores state — it does not. The state lives on the connected node; Web3. js simply communicates with it. Another confusion arises from thinking Web3. js automatically gives you access to user accounts; in browser contexts the wallet injects a provider but you still must call a request to obtain permission. Why this matters: treating Web3. js as a translator simplifies architecture and clarifies where responsibility lies — your dApp forms requests and the provider and node execute them. As you practice, focus on the distinction between the library’s A P I and the provider that actually carries the requests to the network. Can you now explain who sends and who signs transactions in this flow?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Web3.js is the JavaScript library that abstracts RPC and gives dApps an API to read state and send transactions through a provider.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › What is Web3.js?
Definition & metaphor
A translator that turns method calls into RPC traffic the node understands.

Key idea: Web3.js exposes methods to read blockchain data and submit transactions. It does not store blockchain data or run consensus. The node handles that work; Web3.js sends requests and parses responses.

Analogy
Think of Web3.js as a translator between your application and a remote service. Your app speaks JavaScript; the node speaks RPC. Web3.js translates and manages that conversation.
Key Takeaway

Web3.js simplifies interaction with a node; the node executes and stores state. Keep responsibilities separate when designing a dApp.

Concrete example
Fetching a block number and understanding what executes which role.
const Web3 = require('web3');
const web3 = new Web3('http://127.0.0.1:7545');

async function show() {
  const isListening = await web3.eth.net.isListening();
  console.log('listening:', isListening);
  const id = await web3.eth.net.getId();
  console.log('network id:', id);
  const block = await web3.eth.getBlockNumber();
  console.log('latest block:', block);
}

show();
What runs where
Your code calls Web3.js; Web3.js sends RPC to the node; the node responds with data.
Common misconception
Web3.js is not a node and does not sync or validate the chain — it only communicates with one.

screens.title: What is an Ethereum node?
screens.subtitle: Node responsibilities: validation, storage, and network participation

narration.text: An Ethereum node is a machine running client software that synchronizes with the network, validates transactions and blocks, and stores blockchain data. Nodes participate in peer-to-peer gossip, execute transaction logic, and expose RPC interfaces that other programs use to interact with the chain. For development you will often use a local node like Ganache which simulates these behaviors quickly and provides deterministic accounts. In production or when you need reliable public access, hosted node providers maintain full nodes and expose stable endpoints. A common misunderstanding is assuming every developer must run a full node; that is unnecessary for most dApp developers who can rely on hosted services or a light local node during development. Another important point: the node performs the heavy lifting of transaction execution and storage, so when you query state or call contract view functions you are asking the node to return a snapshot of its local chain. Understanding this separation clarifies where to add security controls: signing must occur in a trusted environment or in a wallet controlled by the user, while the node simply relays signed transactions to the network. When you design your app, choose the right node setup for your tolerance for trust, latency, and maintenance.

keyIdea.title: Node role
keyIdea.text: A node stores and validates blockchain data and provides the RPC endpoints that Web3.js uses to query and submit transactions.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Ethereum Node
Ethereum Node Overview
Responsibilities: validation, storage, and providing RPC endpoints.

Nodes synchronize blocks, validate transactions, and expose APIs for querying state. They do not sign transactions on behalf of users; signed transactions are submitted to the node to be propagated and mined.

Local vs Hosted
Local nodes like Ganache are ideal for fast development and deterministic testing. Hosted providers run full infrastructure so you don’t have to maintain it.
Why this matters
Your choice affects latency, trust, operational overhead, and how you handle secrets for signing transactions.
Node architecture (annotated)
Peer network
Gossip and block propagation between nodes.
Execution & storage
State database and EVM execution live here.
RPC endpoints
HTTP or WebSocket APIs that clients use to interact with the node.
Common misconception

You do not need to run a full node to build dApps; many developers use hosted node providers during production and local nodes for development.

screens.title: Provider Types Compared
screens.subtitle: Local node (Ganache) vs Hosted (Infura/Alchemy) vs In-browser (MetaMask)

narration.text: Choosing a provider is a strategic decision. Local providers like Ganache give you an isolated personal blockchain with predictable accounts and fast resets; this is ideal for development and unit testing where you need full control. Hosted providers such as Infura or Alchemy run full node infrastructure and provide stable endpoints for public testnets and mainnet, which reduces operational overhead but introduces trust in the provider’s availability and privacy practices. In-browser providers are supplied by browser wallets like MetaMask via an injected object; they are essential when you need the user to sign transactions and approve account access. A common trade-off question is security versus convenience: hosted providers simplify scale but mean you rely on a third party for connectivity, whereas running your own node gives you independence at the cost of maintenance. Practically, use Ganache during development, use hosted providers for broader public connectivity, and integrate MetaMask for user-driven signing flows in the browser. When you test, ensure you mimic the final environment: if users will use MetaMask in production, practice the injected provider flow during your browser tests so permission prompts and eth_requestAccounts behavior are correct.

keyIdea.title: Provider trade-offs
keyIdea.text: Local nodes offer control and speed for development; hosted providers offer scalability and reduced maintenance; browser providers enable user signing and account consent.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Provider Types
Local — Ganache
Personal blockchain for development. Fast, resettable, deterministic accounts.
  • Typical URL: http://127.0.0.1:7545
  • Use for contract development and tests
Hosted — Infura / Alchemy
Managed node infrastructure for public testnets and mainnet. Highly available but third-party trust required.
  • Use HTTPS endpoints with a project ID
  • Good for production dApps that need scale
In-browser — MetaMask
Injected provider that enables user account access and signing within the browser environment.
  • Requires explicit user permission via eth_requestAccounts
  • Essential for end-user transaction signing
Decision checklist
Development speed → Ganache
Production scale → Hosted
User signing → In-browser

screens.title: Setting up Web3.js in Node.js
screens.subtitle: Importing Web3, creating an instance, and verifying connectivity

narration.text: Let's walk through the canonical Node. js setup: import Web3, provide a provider URL, create a new instance, and run simple network checks. In practice you install the package, require or import the constructor, and pass a provider string such as a local Ganache URL or a hosted HTTPS endpoint. After creating the instance, use isListening to confirm the node responds, then getId and getBlockNumber to verify the network identity and current state. A common mistake is forgetting to await asynchronous calls — this causes a pending Promise to be printed instead of the actual result. Another pitfall is using an incorrect provider URL: check the protocol, host, and port carefully. In a production app you might wrap these calls in try... catch blocks to surface connection errors and give actionable messages. For example, if isListening returns false or throws, log the provider URL to help diagnose whether the node is offline or a network rule blocks the request. Following this setup pattern creates a reliable connectivity baseline for further contract interactions. Setting up Web3.js in Node.js means install web3, create a new web3 instance with a provider url, and run islistening, getid, and getblocknumber to verify connectivity.. In practical terms, importing web3, creating an instance, and verifying connectivity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Node setup
keyIdea.text: Install Web3, create a new Web3 instance with a provider URL, and run isListening, getId, and getBlockNumber to verify connectivity.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Setup in Node.js
Step-by-step setup
Install, import, create instance, verify listening and network ID.
// First, install web3: npm install web3
const Web3 = require('web3');

const providerUrl = 'http://127.0.0.1:7545';
const web3 = new Web3(providerUrl);

async function verify() {
  try {
    const isListening = await web3.eth.net.isListening();
    console.log('Connected:', isListening);
    if (isListening) {
      const networkId = await web3.eth.net.getId();
      const blockNumber = await web3.eth.getBlockNumber();
      console.log('Network ID:', networkId, 'Block:', blockNumber);
    }
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Connection error:', err.message);
  }
}

verify();
Explanation & tips
  • Use await because these methods return Promises; otherwise you’ll see pending results.
  • Wrap calls in try...catch to handle unreachable providers or timeouts gracefully.
  • Log the provider URL in error messages to help debugging.
Common mistake

Printing the Promise instead of awaiting it. Always await asynchronous web3 calls inside an async function.

screens.title: Connecting to Ganache (Local Node)
screens.subtitle: Start Ganache, connect with a provider URL, and verify the connection

narration.text: Working with Ganache is a fast, repeatable workflow for contract development. Start the Ganache desktop app or run ganache-cli to create a local chain endpoint, usually listening at http://127.0.0.1:7545. Your dApp simply points Web3 to that URL. After creating the Web3 instance, run isListening to confirm the node accepts connections, then fetch the network ID and block number for additional verification. If the node is not running you will see connection errors or timeouts; check that Ganache is active and that no firewall blocks the port. An example terminal sequence is: start Ganache, run your Node. js script, and observe console output that confirms listening and prints the network ID and block number. A common trap is copying a provider URL with an incorrect protocol or port; always verify the exact endpoint Ganache reports. Finally, remember that Ganache provides unlocked test accounts — never reuse these accounts for real funds, they are only for local development. This safe environment enables fast iterations and deterministic tests before switching to a hosted testnet provider. Connecting to Ganache (Local Node) means run ganache to provide a local http endpoint, connect web3 to that url, and verify connectivity with islistening and network checks.. In practical terms, start ganache, connect with a provider url, and verify the connection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Ganache workflow
keyIdea.text: Run Ganache to provide a local HTTP endpoint, connect Web3 to that URL, and verify connectivity with isListening and network checks.

Quick steps
  1. Start Ganache on your machine so it serves at http://127.0.0.1:7545.
  2. Create a Web3 instance using that URL.
  3. Call isListening, then getId and getBlockNumber to confirm.

Ganache test accounts are unsecured for development only. Do not use them with real funds or public networks.

Network ID: 5777
Current Block Number: 7

If you see a connection error, confirm Ganache is running and that the provider URL matches the Ganache interface exactly.

screens.title: Connecting to Hosted Providers (Infura/Alchemy)
screens.subtitle: Using HTTPS endpoints and project IDs to access public networks

narration.text: Hosted providers like Infura and Alchemy manage full node infrastructure and expose HTTPS endpoints you can use from Node or server environments. To use them you obtain a project ID from the provider dashboard and construct an HTTPS URL that includes that ID. Then pass that URL to the Web3 constructor in place of a local URL. Hosted endpoints are convenient because they abstract node maintenance, provide stable uptime, and often support multiple networks. A practice point: treat your project ID like a configuration secret and do not hard-code it into client-side bundles that run in the browser. For testing, you can use a hosted testnet endpoint to connect to Sepolia or other public testnets. When you verify the connection, expect the same sequence of calls: isListening, getId, and getBlockNumber. If you get a network or authentication error, check the project ID, whether the provider restricts IPs or referrers, and whether you selected the correct network in the URL. Hosted providers may also expose usage dashboards that help diagnose rate limiting or credential issues. Connecting to Hosted Providers (Infura/Alchemy) means hosted providers offer stable endpoints for public networks; use a project id and protected configuration, and verify connectivity the same way as with local nodes.. In practical terms, using https endpoints and project ids to access public networks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hosted access
keyIdea.text: Hosted providers offer stable endpoints for public networks; use a project ID and protected configuration, and verify connectivity the same way as with local nodes.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Hosted Providers
How to initialize Web3 with Infura
// Example using Infura
const infuraProvider = 'https://sepolia.infura.io/v3/YOUR_INFURA_PROJECT_ID';
const web3 = new Web3(infuraProvider);

// Then verify with isListening and getId
Keep your project ID in environment configuration; avoid shipping it inside client-side bundles that expose credentials.
Troubleshooting hosted connections
  • Authentication errors often mean a wrong or revoked project ID.
  • Rate limiting or blocked referrers can prevent responses; check the provider dashboard.
  • Hosted providers may require HTTPS; ensure protocol is correct.
Why it matters

Hosted providers enable production-grade access without node maintenance, but they shift trust and may require careful credential management.

screens.title: window.ethereum and browser wallets
screens.subtitle: How MetaMask injects a provider and how to request account access

narration.text: When a user runs a browser wallet such as MetaMask, the wallet typically injects a provider object into the window under the name window. ethereum. This object serves as the provider for Web3. js and routes requests through the user’s wallet, allowing the user to approve transactions and sign data. Your dApp must explicitly request account access by calling the wallet’s request method with the appropriate permission name, which triggers a UI prompt for the user. Always wrap this call in a try... catch block because the user may deny access; your app should handle that gracefully by informing the user of the missing permission and disabling operations that require signing. A common mistake is assuming window. ethereum is available immediately; check for its presence before using it. Another important point: do not expose private keys in the browser. Let the wallet manage signing so the user’s secret stays protected. Testing browser flows ensures permission prompts and account selection behave as expected when you move from local tests to real users. window.ethereum and browser wallets means browser wallets inject window.ethereum which the dapp must request permission from to access accounts and perform user-driven signing.. In practical terms, how metamask injects a provider and how to request account access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: In-browser provider
keyIdea.text: Browser wallets inject window.ethereum which the dApp must request permission from to access accounts and perform user-driven signing.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Browser Provider
Typical flow in a browser dApp
Detect window.ethereum, request account access, then create Web3 with the injected provider.
User consent
Calling the permission request triggers a wallet prompt; handle denials and errors cleanly.
Developer checks
  • Always check for the existence of an injected provider before using it.
  • Wrap requests in try...catch to catch user rejection and other errors.
  • Do not assume a single account; wallets may expose multiple accounts or switch them.
Common pitfall

Assuming window.ethereum exists in every browser session. Always code defensively and provide fallbacks or clear instructions to users.

screens.title: Common connection errors
screens.subtitle: Unreachable provider, wrong URL, missing await, and absent injected provider

narration.text: When a connection fails, the error typically points to one of a small set of root causes. First, an unreachable provider often means the node is not running or the wrong port is used; if Ganache is stopped you will see connection timeouts or network errors. Second, an incorrect provider URL — wrong protocol, host, or port — will prevent successful requests; double-check the exact endpoint printed by your node. Third, forgetting to await asynchronous Web3 calls results in pending Promises instead of actual values; this is a common developer error in Node scripts and tests. Fourth, in browser contexts the injected provider might be absent because the user doesn’t have a wallet installed or has denied permissions. To diagnose, add clear logging that prints the provider URL and wrap calls in try... catch to display actionable messages. Also consider network-level issues such as firewalls or proxy settings that block HTTP or WebSocket traffic. A practical troubleshooting sequence is: confirm node is running, verify the provider URL, test with curl or a simple script, and inspect console errors for authentication or rate-limiting messages. This stepwise approach makes most connection problems straightforward to resolve.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting
keyIdea.text: Diagnose failures by checking node availability, provider URL correctness, proper use of await, and the presence of injected providers in browsers.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Connection Errors
Unreachable provider
Ensure the node is running and check the exact host and port reported by the node.
Wrong URL or protocol
Verify http vs https and the project ID for hosted providers.
Missing await
If you see Promise { } you likely forgot to await an async call.
Diagnostic checklist
  1. Confirm node process is running.
  2. Compare the provider URL to the node listing.
  3. Run a simple script that calls isListening and logs errors.
  4. Check browser console for missing injected provider or user rejection.
Pro tip

Add clear provider URL logging and error messages in your app to speed up diagnosis. Always test the path your app will use in production.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Activity
Starter Code (connect.js)
const Web3 = require('web3');

async function connectToBlockchain() {
    // TODO: Define the Ganache provider URL
    const providerUrl = 'http://127.0.0.1:7545'; 

    // TODO: Create a new Web3 instance with the provider
    const web3 = new Web3(providerUrl);

    try {
        // TODO: Check if the node is listening and log the result
        const isListening = await web3.eth.net.isListening();
        console.log('Is connected to Ethereum node:', isListening);

        if (isListening) {
            // TODO: Get the network ID and log it
            const networkId = await web3.eth.net.getId();
            console.log('Connected to Network ID:', networkId);

            // Get the current block number as an extra check
            const blockNumber = await web3.eth.getBlockNumber();
            console.log('Current Block Number:', blockNumber);
        } else {
            console.error('Failed to connect to the Ethereum node.');
        }
    } catch (error) {
        console.error('An error occurred during connection:', error.message);
        console.error('Please ensure Ganache is running on', providerUrl);
    }
}

connectToBlockchain();
Activity checklist
  1. Create a new directory and run npm init -y.
  2. Install Web3.js with npm install web3.
  3. Start Ganache and run node connect.js to verify output.
  4. Stop Ganache and run the script again to observe the error handling path.
Expected outcome

When Ganache runs, the script prints connected true, the network ID, and the current block number. When Ganache is down, the script logs a connection error with the provider URL for debugging.

screens.title: Asynchronous calls and awaiting results
screens.subtitle: Why most Web3.js methods return Promises and how to handle them

narration.text: Most interactions with a blockchain are asynchronous: network requests take time and nodes respond when they are ready. Web3. js therefore exposes many methods that return Promises. This design requires you to mark your functions as asynchronous and use await or then to obtain actual values. A frequent beginner error is calling a method and immediately logging its return value without awaiting, which prints a pending Promise object rather than the expected number or data structure. A concrete example is calling the block number method; using await yields the numeric block height, while omitting it yields an unresolved Promise. Another subtle point is error handling: network or provider errors are surfaced as rejected Promises, so wrap awaits in try... catch to present user-friendly messages and avoid unhandled promise rejections. In longer-running apps, use timeouts and retries prudently when nodes may be slow. Finally, when you write tests or demo scripts, always await state queries to ensure deterministic outputs. Practicing a small script that intentionally omits await, then fixes it, is the fastest way to internalize this pattern. Asynchronous calls and awaiting results means web3.js methods are asynchronous and return promises; always await them inside async functions and handle errors with try...catch for robust code.. In practical terms, why most web3.js methods return promises and how to handle them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Async handling
keyIdea.text: Web3.js methods are asynchronous and return Promises; always await them inside async functions and handle errors with try...catch for robust code.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Async & Await
Incorrect pattern
const block = web3.eth.getBlockNumber();
console.log(block); // Promise {  }
This happens because the call returns a Promise. The value is not yet available synchronously.
Correct pattern
async function showBlock() {
  const block = await web3.eth.getBlockNumber();
  console.log(block); // 12345
}
Key takeaway

Await Promise-returning methods and use try...catch to gracefully handle failures.

narration.text: Here are the essential concepts to carry forward. Web3. js is the JavaScript library that provides an easy A P I to read blockchain state and send transactions; remember it does not store or validate the chain. An Ethereum node runs the client software, holds the chain data, and serves RPC endpoints that clients use. Providers are the connection points between Web3. js and nodes; pick local, hosted, or in-browser providers depending on development speed, scale, and whether the user signs transactions. Ganache is the recommended local test chain for quick iterations. Infura and Alchemy are examples of hosted providers that give scalable access to public networks, but they introduce third-party trust considerations. Keep these core ideas in mind as you practice connecting, verifying isListening and network ID, and handling asynchronous calls correctly. These foundations make higher-level contract work possible and debuggable.

Practice creating Web3 instances with local and hosted providers, confirm connectivity, and handle async calls correctly. These are the minimum skills needed for reliable dApp development.

narration.text: A few practical reminders: use Ganache for local testing because it gives predictable accounts and quick resets; treat hosted providers like Infura or Alchemy as production-grade endpoints but keep credentials out of client bundles; and remember that window. ethereum enables user-driven signing in the browser but requires explicit permission from the user. Also be aware of RPC as the underlying protocol used to send and receive requests between Web3. js and a node. When you troubleshoot, follow a stepwise process: confirm the node is running, verify the provider URL, ensure you await asynchronous calls, and check for injected providers or permission denials in browser contexts. These checks catch the majority of common errors and will make your dApp’s network layer reliable and predictable. Reflect on the security trade-offs of using hosted providers versus running your own node and how that affects privacy and operational responsibility.

keyIdea.title: Practical reminders
